summary:
Zamfara operates its own Sharia criminal-law layer in addition to Nigeria's national framework. The state's governor was the first in Nigeria to move, promulgating the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. The enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, was enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution; it established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code.

The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture applied by the Sharia courts of the twelve northern states, a framework Zamfara pioneered. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those states remain the only ones in Nigeria where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

For a visitor, the operative consequence is that criminal cases in Zamfara can be heard by Sharia courts applying codified Islamic criminal law, a track separate from the national statute. The state's courts are the venue in which Sharia criminal penalties would be imposed locally.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on the extension of Sharia to criminal law documents Zamfara's adoption as the opening move in the process. The state's then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, set out Zamfara's own account of the adoption at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000.

A committee appointed by the governor in June 1999 was mandated to study implementing Sharia, including the full scope of Islamic criminal law. By the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia.
localsOnly:
The Grand Kadi took over administration of Zamfara's Sharia courts on 29 June 2000. The state's codified Sharia Penal Code sets the offences and punishments those courts apply, and residents' criminal cases can be heard under it.

The adoption was accompanied by policy moves against prostitution and gambling, indicating the enforcement priorities of the state institutions that administer the Sharia regime.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record Zamfara-specific enforcement of the Sharia Penal Code against trans or gender-nonconforming people, nor arrest or prosecution figures for the state. The state's Sharia Penal Code provisions on same-sex conduct are not set out in the available material.

The principal sources on Zamfara's Sharia adoption date from 1999 to 2004 and describe the framework's establishment rather than its current application; no recent state-level enforcement record is sourced here.
